entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henri de Valenciennes was a 13th-century French writer, historian, and chronicler of the Latin Empire, born in the early 13th century but exact dates unknown. He is considered one of the most important chroniclers of the Latin Empire, which was a short-lived Christian state in the Eastern Mediterranean.


De Valenciennes' works are significant for their detailed account of the empire's history, including its founding by Emperor Baldwin II in 1171 and its eventual fall to the Ottoman Empire in 1278. His chronicle, known as the 'Chronicle of Henri de Valenciennes', provides valuable insights into the empire's politics, society, and culture during this period.


De Valenciennes' legacy extends beyond his own writings, as his chronicle has served as a primary source for historians studying the Latin Empire and its impact on the region.


One striking statistic is that the Latin Empire's territory covered a vast area of approximately 70,000 square miles, stretching from the Aegean Sea to the Black Sea.


A direct attributed quote from De Valenciennes' chronicle illustrates his meticulous attention to detail: 'The Emperor Baldwin II, in the year 1171, founded the city of Nicaea, which became the capital of the Latin Empire.'
